task: I'm the director of the St. Anne's community choir and we have 5 new members joining tomorrow night's rehearsal. Write a warm welcome message I can read aloud before we start, mentioning we rehearse Tuesdays at 7pm and that our spring concert is in April.

agency: The raw material is the director's own voice and the choir's real details. The sign-up sheet names the five newcomers and the folder holds tomorrow's first piece, but neither is in reach. acceleration: Write for the ear, not the page. Use short sentences, one idea per breath, and a rule of three where it lands naturally. Target about a minute at speaking pace, roughly 130 to 150 words.

accuracy: Nothing outside the model can check a spoken welcome. The closest proxy is that the director reads it aloud once and trims whatever trips the tongue. The fixed facts are the ones given: St. Anne's community choir, five new members, Tuesdays at 7pm, spring concert in April.

answers.plain:
Here's a welcome you can read aloud:

---

Good evening, everyone, and welcome to St. Anne's Community Choir!

Before we begin, I'd like to take a moment to welcome our five new members who are joining us tonight. We're so glad you're here. Whether you've sung for years or are stepping into a choir for the very first time, you belong in this room, and your voice makes ours stronger.

A few quick things to know: we meet every Tuesday at 7pm, and we'll be working toward our spring concert in April. There's plenty of time to learn the music, grow together, and have a lot of fun along the way.

Don't worry if things feel unfamiliar at first. Everyone here remembers their first night, and our longtime members are happy to help with anything, from finding your place in the music to figuring out where the tea is kept.

So, to our new members: welcome, welcome, welcome. Let's make some music together!

---

It should take about 45 seconds to read. If you'd like, I can add a line introducing the new members by name, mention the section leaders, or adjust the tone to be more formal or more playful.
answers.nudge:
# Welcome script for tomorrow night (about 90 seconds)

*Stand, wait for the room to settle, and smile before you begin.*

Good evening, everyone. Before we sing a note, I'd like to take a minute to welcome five people who are joining us tonight.

*(Gesture toward the new members.)*

Would our new members stand up, or just wave? Let's give them a proper St. Anne's welcome.

*(Pause for applause.)*

Thank you for coming. Walking into a room full of people who already know each other takes a little courage. Every one of us has been in your seat, and we're very glad you chose ours.

Here's what you need to know. We rehearse **every Tuesday at 7pm**. You'll hear me say this a lot: you don't need to be perfect. You only need to show up, listen, and enjoy it. Nobody here expects you to know everything tonight. If you get lost, follow the person next to you. If you're still lost, smile and keep going. That's what the rest of us do.

We're working toward our **spring concert in April**. That gives us plenty of time to learn the music and grow together as a sound. By then, you won't just be watching from the back. You'll be part of it, standing on stage with us.

A choir is a strange and wonderful thing. Each person brings one voice. Together we make something none of us could make alone. So tonight, you're not just joining a group. You're adding a part that wasn't here before.

To our returning members: please look after our newcomers tonight. Introduce yourselves at the break, share a folder if you need to, and tell them where the tea is.

*(Beat.)*

Right. Let's sing.

---

## Short version (about 20 seconds)

"Before we begin, please join me in welcoming our five new members. We're so glad you're here. We meet every Tuesday at 7pm, and we're building toward our spring concert in April, where you'll be on stage with us. You don't need to be perfect, just curious and willing. Welcome to the St. Anne's family. Now, let's sing."

---

## Professional touches

- **Use names.** If you have the five names, add: "Please welcome Maria, Tom, …" Hearing their names aloud makes people feel seen far more than a general welcome does.
- **Pair each newcomer with a buddy.** Before the speech, ask five steady members to sit beside the new people. Then add the line "Your buddy tonight is the person on your left."
- **Put the break to use.** Mention one practical item, such as where to find music or tea, or who to ask about folders and dues. New members mostly worry about small logistics.
- **Start with something easy.** Open the first warm-up with a simple, familiar piece so newcomers hear themselves blend in within the first five minutes.
- **Speak slowly.** Nerves speed people up. Pause after "Tuesdays at 7pm" and "April" so the details sink in.
- **Follow up.** Send a short note to the five on Wednesday: "So glad you joined us. See you next Tuesday at 7pm." It makes it much more likely they come back.

If you give me the concert date, the venue, and the new members' names, I can tailor the script to them.

Good evening, everyone.

Welcome to St. Anne's community choir.

It's good to see you all here tonight.

First, a special hello to our five new members. We're so glad you've come.

Welcome. Truly.

We rehearse here every Tuesday at seven. Same room, same time, same friendly faces.

You'll find your place quickly.

Now, I know walking into a new room can feel a little daunting. So let me say this plainly.

There is no pressure tonight.

None at all.

You don't need to be perfect. You don't need to know everything. Just listen, join in when you're ready, and enjoy the sound.

You're standing among friends here.

Every person in this room was new once. We remember that feeling. And we promise to make it easy.

Looking ahead, our spring concert is in April.

That's a lovely thing to work toward together. And you'll be a part of it.

But that's for later.

Tonight is simply about singing.

So let's begin.

Feet flat on the floor. Shoulders soft. Take a slow, easy breath in...

And let's warm up our voices together.
